title: Muscle Energy Technique, Myofascial Techniques and Strain-Counterstrain

blocks.text: The patient performs a gentle, controlled contraction against the therapist's resistance, followed by relaxation and movement into new range.

rows: Take the muscle to its first barrier; patient contracts the same muscle gently (about 10 to 20% effort) for 5 to 10 s; relax; move to the new barrier; repeat 3 to 5 times
When the target muscle is painful to contract

blocks.text: Effects on range are likely from increased stretch tolerance rather than true muscle lengthening [Ref – to verify].

**Example (hamstrings PIR)**: patient supine; raise the straight leg to the first resistance; patient pushes the heel gently toward the couch for 7 s; relax and breathe out; lift to the new barrier; repeat 3 to 5 times.

sections.title: B. Myofascial techniques and trigger points

items: **Myofascial trigger points**: hyperirritable spots in a taut band of muscle that can refer pain. Their nature and diagnosis remain debated, with limited reliability [Ref – to verify].
**Ischaemic compression**: sustained pressure on a tender point until discomfort reduces (about 30 to 90 s). **Myofascial release**: slow, sustained stretch and pressure on soft tissue.
**Dry needling**: requires specific training and licensing according to local regulation.

blocks.text: Evidence: short-term pain relief in some conditions; best used with exercise [Ref – to verify].

items: Find a tender point and rate tenderness as 10 out of 10.
Move the body passively into a position of comfort (often shortening the tissue) until tenderness falls by at least 70% (to 3 out of 10 or less).
Hold about 90 seconds while monitoring the point.
Return slowly and passively to neutral; reassess.

blocks.text: Useful for highly irritable patients who cannot tolerate other techniques.

rows: Local tender muscle point reproducing familiar pain
Ischaemic compression or myofascial technique, followed by active exercise

items: **How strong is the contraction in PIR?** Gentle, about 10 to 20% effort.
**What is the endpoint in strain-counterstrain positioning?** At least a 70% reduction in tenderness.
**Which technique suits a highly irritable acute neck?** Strain-counterstrain.
**Why add exercise after soft-tissue techniques?** To maintain gains and build capacity.
**What explains range gains after MET?** Mainly increased stretch tolerance.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Apply PIR, ischaemic compression and strain-counterstrain.
Choose the right soft-tissue approach for the presentation.
